section.title: Daily and Festival Offerings
section.sectionRationale: As Israel prepares to leave the wilderness rhythm behind and settle in the land, God re-establishes the rhythm of worship that must continue there: daily offerings, weekly Sabbath offerings, monthly new moon offerings, and the great annual feasts. Settlement does not mean the end of dependence on God's appointed worship; it means carrying it into a new home.
section.thesis: The LORD commands Israel to keep a continual rhythm of offerings, daily morning and evening, weekly on the Sabbath, monthly at the new moon, and at the yearly feasts of Passover, Unleavened Bread, and Firstfruits, each a pleasing aroma to the LORD, sustaining Israel's worship life once they enter and settle the land.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the daily burnt offering morning and evening; the added offerings for the Sabbath and the new moon; the Passover and the seven days of Unleavened Bread; and the day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Command the Israelites and say to them: See that you present to Me at its appointed time the food for My offerings by fire, as a {{aroma|pleasing aroma}} to Me.
And tell them that this is the offering made by fire you are to present to the LORD as a regular burnt offering each day: two unblemished year-old male lambs.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight,
along with a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a grain offering, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives.
This is a regular burnt offering established at Mount Sinai as a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.
The drink offering accompanying each lamb shall be a quarter hin. Pour out the offering of fermented drink to the LORD in the sanctuary area.
And offer the second lamb at twilight, with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning. It is an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

units.label: The Sabbath and new moon offerings
units.note: in addition to the regular burnt offering

verses.text: On the Sabbath day, present two unblemished year-old male lambs, accompanied by a grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, as well as a drink offering.
This is the burnt offering for every Sabbath, in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.
At the beginning of every month, you are to present to the LORD a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering with each bull, two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering with the ram,
and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering with each lamb. This is a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine with each bull, a third of a hin with the ram, and a quarter hin with each lamb. This is the monthly burnt offering to be made at each new moon throughout the year.
In addition to the regular burnt offering with its drink offering, one male goat is to be presented to the LORD as a sin offering.
The fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover.
On the fifteenth day of this month, there shall be a feast; for seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten.
On the first day there is to be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.
Present to the LORD an offering made by fire, a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished.
The grain offering shall consist of fine flour mixed with oil; offer three-tenths of an ephah with each bull, two-tenths of an ephah with the ram,
and a tenth of an ephah with each of the seven lambs.
Include one male goat as a sin offering to make {{atonement|atonement}} for you.
You are to present these in addition to the regular morning burnt offering.
Offer the same food each day for seven days as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It is to be offered with its drink offering and the regular burnt offering.
On the seventh day you shall hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.
On the day of firstfruits, when you present an offering of new grain to the LORD during the Feast of Weeks, you are to hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.
Present a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old as a pleasing aroma to the LORD,
together with their grain offerings of fine flour mixed with oil, three-tenths of an ephah with each bull, two-tenths of an ephah with the ram,
and a tenth of an ephah with each of the seven lambs.
Include one male goat to make atonement for you.
Offer them with their drink offerings in addition to the regular burnt offering and its grain offering. The animals must be unblemished.

aroma.gloss: A pleasing, soothing aroma. The phrase repeats throughout this chapter, describing how faithful, obedient worship is received by God, not because He needs the smoke of a sacrifice but because it represents the costly, fragrant devotion of a heart given to Him.

atonement.gloss: To atone, to cover, to make amends for sin. The sin offering accompanying each festival provides kaphar, atonement, reminding Israel that even joyful worship at appointed feasts still requires a covering for sin before it can be rightly offered.

basic.context: As Israel stands ready to leave the wilderness and enter the land, God lays out the rhythm of worship that must continue there: daily offerings morning and evening, extra offerings each Sabbath and new moon, and the greater festivals of Passover, Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Weeks. Settling in the land does not mean settling into casual worship.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, detailed set of ceremonial laws for Israel's sacrificial system, not primarily moral instruction for readers today. Its purpose is to establish a sustained, disciplined rhythm of worship, layered daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly, that would carry Israel's dependence on God's provision from the wilderness into permanent settlement.
basic.originalLanguages: Each offering is called a reach nichoach, a pleasing aroma, language repeated throughout the chapter to describe worship that pleases God when offered in faithful obedience. Alongside nearly every festival offering stands a sin offering to make kaphar, atonement, showing that even Israel's most joyful national celebrations required a covering for sin before God.
basic.typology: The unblemished lambs offered morning and evening, without fail, every single day of the year, anticipate the perfect, once-for-all sacrifice of Christ, the Lamb of God, whose single offering ends the need for this daily repetition, Hebrews 10:11-14.
basic.christ: Hebrews 10 explicitly contrasts the daily, repeated offerings of this system, offered again and again yet never able to take away sins, with the single sacrifice of Christ, who by one offering has perfected forever those who are being sanctified; every unblemished lamb offered morning and evening here points toward the spotless Lamb who was offered once, completely.
basic.god: God cares about the rhythm of worship, not leaving it to spontaneous whim but establishing a fixed, generous structure that keeps His people returning to Him daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly. His holiness requires a sin offering even at times of festival joy, yet His provision of that offering shows His readiness to keep His people close to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 10:1-14 contrasts these repeated offerings with Christ's single, sufficient sacrifice. John 1:29 names Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, echoing the unblemished lambs of this chapter. 1 Corinthians 5:7 calls Christ our Passover lamb, sacrificed for us, drawing directly on the festival named here.
basic.oneStory: Israel's worship life was structured around constant, repeated offerings, daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly, each requiring an unblemished sacrifice and, often, atonement for sin. That entire structure, repeated because it could never finally remove sin, points forward to the one, sufficient sacrifice of Christ, who fulfills and ends the need for endless repetition.

context.literary:
Numbers 28 opens a two chapter calendar that runs through Numbers 29 and closes with a summary, 'You are to present these offerings to the LORD at your appointed times,' Numbers 29:39. Chapter 28 covers the daily offering, verses 3 to 8, the Sabbath, verses 9 to 10, the new moon, verses 11 to 15, Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, verses 16 to 25, and the day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks, verses 26 to 31. Chapter 29 then covers the seventh month.

The organising principle is the offering itself. Leviticus 23 sets out the same feasts from the worshipper's side, with dates, rest and rituals such as the wave sheaf and the booths. Numbers 28 and 29 set them out from the altar's side, specifying what animals, how much flour, how much oil and how much wine are to be offered on each occasion. The two chapters complement each other rather than repeat.

A single refrain holds the chapter together: 'in addition to the regular burnt offering,' verses 10, 15, 23 and 31, with a variation in verse 24. Every weekly, monthly and yearly offering is layered on top of the daily one. The morning and evening lamb never stops for a festival; the festival is added to it. The structure itself says that the special days rest on the ordinary ones.

There is also a clear numerical pattern. The daily offering is two lambs; the Sabbath doubles it. The new moon, each day of Unleavened Bread and the day of firstfruits share one standard set: two bulls, one ram, seven lambs and a male goat for a sin offering. Seven recurs throughout, seven lambs, seven days, the seventh day.

The placement matters. The new generation has just been numbered, the question of inheritance settled and Joshua commissioned. Now God gives them the rhythm of worship for the land. Only three chapters earlier the old generation had eaten the sacrifices of Moab's gods at Peor, Numbers 25:2. The calendar of chapter 28 is God's answer: these are His appointed times and His offerings.
context.historical:
Verse 6 says the regular burnt offering was 'established at Mount Sinai,' pointing back to Exodus 29:38 to 42, where the daily lambs were first commanded. The regulation is repeated here because a new generation must take it into the land. Much of what it requires, fine flour, pressed olive oil and wine, belongs to settled farming rather than wandering. Numbers 15:2 had already framed such offerings with the words 'After you enter the land.'

The measures are modest but constant. The BSB footnotes estimate a tenth of an ephah of flour at about two dry quarts, and a quarter hin of oil or wine at about one quart. Over a year the daily offering alone required more than seven hundred lambs, before any Sabbath, new moon or feast was added. Worship at the tabernacle represented a real and continual gift from the nation's flocks and fields.

The morning and evening offerings framed Israel's day. 'At twilight' is literally 'between the two evenings,' as the footnote to verse 4 notes, the same expression used for the Passover slaughter in Exodus 12:6. Elijah prayed on Carmel 'at the time of the evening sacrifice,' 1 Kings 18:36, and David asked that his uplifted hands be 'like the evening offering,' Psalm 141:2. Incense was burned at the same hours, Exodus 30:7 to 8.

The calendar was kept, neglected and restored across Israel's history. Solomon built the temple for burnt offerings 'every morning and evening as well as on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts,' 2 Chronicles 2:4 and 8:13. Hezekiah funded them from his own possessions, 2 Chronicles 31:3. After the exile the returned community rebuilt the altar and resumed 'the regular burnt offerings,' Ezra 3:5, and bound itself by oath to support them, Nehemiah 10:33. Daniel foresaw a time when an enemy would remove 'His daily sacrifice,' Daniel 8:11 and 12:11, a sign of the gravest desecration.
context.canonical:
The rhythm of Numbers 28 runs through the rest of Scripture. The triad of Sabbath, new moon and appointed feast became a standard way of naming Israel's worship, 2 Chronicles 2:4 and Nehemiah 10:33. The prophets used the same triad to expose hollow worship. Isaiah hears God say, 'your New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations. I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly,' Isaiah 1:13, and Hosea 2:11 threatens to end 'her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths.' Yet Isaiah also looks forward to a day when 'From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me,' Isaiah 66:23. Ezekiel's restored temple keeps a daily lamb every morning, Ezekiel 46:13 to 15.

The Psalms interiorise the sacrifices. 'May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering,' Psalm 141:2. 'The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,' Psalm 51:17. Psalm 50:12 to 13 corrects any idea that God eats: 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you.'

The New Testament names the same three terms and calls them a shadow. 'Let no one judge you... with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16 to 17. Hebrews contrasts the daily ministry of priests who 'offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins,' Hebrews 10:11, with Christ's one sacrifice, and it notes that He 'does not need to offer daily sacrifices,' Hebrews 7:27. Paul calls Christ 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The Spirit is poured out 'when the day of Pentecost came,' Acts 2:1, the Feast of Weeks of verse 26, as the BSB footnote notes. And the vocabulary of the offerings is carried over into Christian life: 'a fragrant sacrificial offering,' Ephesians 5:2, 'living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1, and 'a sacrifice of praise,' offered 'continually,' Hebrews 13:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wanted the generation about to enter Canaan to understand that life in the land would be organised around God. The first hearers had grown up in the wilderness, where the tabernacle stood in the middle of the camp and God's presence went before them. In the land they would scatter to farms and towns, and the danger was that worship would become occasional. Chapter 28 sets a rhythm that makes that impossible: every day, every week, every month and every season returns Israel to the altar.

He also wanted them to understand whose worship it was. God calls these 'My offerings,' 'My food' and 'its appointed time,' verse 2. Israel does not invent its calendar; it receives one. After the disaster at Peor, where the people accepted an invitation to the sacrifices of other gods, the point is sharp. Israel's table and Israel's festivals belong to the LORD.

Finally, he wanted them to know that joy and atonement belong together. The new moon, the week of Unleavened Bread and the day of firstfruits all include a male goat 'to make atonement for you,' verses 22 and 30. The first hearers were to celebrate God's provision as forgiven people, with sin dealt with before they feasted.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These are commands, and for Israel under the Sinai covenant they were binding. Numbers 28 prescribes; it does not merely describe. But the New Testament tells us how such commands now apply. The sacrifices themselves are fulfilled in Christ, who 'sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself,' Hebrews 7:27. Christians are told not to let anyone judge them regarding 'a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath,' because these were 'a shadow' whose substance is Christ, Colossians 2:16 to 17. The church therefore does not offer lambs or keep this calendar as law.

What remains is the principle that worship is regular, given by God and shaped by His provision. Believers are to offer 'a sacrifice of praise' continually, Hebrews 13:15, to present their bodies as 'living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1, and to 'Pray without ceasing,' 1 Thessalonians 5:17. The rhythm of morning and evening, of a day set apart each week, and of gathering to remember the Lord's death all carry the spirit of this chapter into Christian life, though not its letter.

debates.question: Why does nearly every festival offering include a sin offering even at joyful celebrations?

views.label: Sin offerings maintained ongoing purification necessary for any approach to a holy God
views.case: The festivals took place before the LORD's dwelling. The sin offering cleansed the sanctuary and the people from the defilement that sin brings, so the community stayed fit to worship. The pattern of the new moon, verse 15, and of the feasts, verses 22 and 30, shows that no season was exempt.

views.label: The offerings taught that celebration and repentance are not opposites
views.case: By placing a goat for atonement in the middle of festival joy, the law taught Israel that gladness before God flows from being forgiven, not from forgetting sin. The Lord's Supper holds the same pairing: a feast that proclaims a death, Luke 22:19 to 20.

debates.bearing: Both readings point to the same conclusion Hebrews draws: the repeated sin offerings were 'an annual reminder of sins,' Hebrews 10:3, which shows that they could not finally remove sin. Christ's single sacrifice both cleanses and gladdens, so the church's feast is kept as forgiven people.

debates.question: In what sense are the offerings God's 'food'?

views.label: Borrowed language that Scripture itself corrects
views.case: Israel's neighbours imagined their gods eating sacrifices. Scripture uses the language, 'My food,' verse 2, and 'the food of their God,' Leviticus 21:6, but denies the idea: 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you... Do I eat the flesh of bulls?' Psalm 50:12 to 13. The phrase is a picture, not a claim about divine need.

views.label: Covenant hospitality at God's table
views.case: The offerings are presented at the tent where God dwells among His people, Exodus 29:45. Calling them God's food frames worship as a meal in the house of the covenant Lord, where Israel brings the best of its land to the King who gave it. Many offerings were in fact shared with priests and worshippers.

debates.bearing: The two views agree that God needs nothing. The language of food expresses fellowship and honour, not hunger. That is why the New Testament can speak of 'an altar' from which believers eat, Hebrews 13:10, and why the fitting response to a God who needs nothing is thanksgiving, Psalm 50:14.

debates.question: What time of day is meant by 'at twilight,' literally 'between the two evenings'?

views.label: The period between sunset and full darkness
views.case: On this reading the first evening is sunset and the second is nightfall, and the lamb was offered in the short time between. It keeps close to the most natural sense of 'evening.'

views.label: The afternoon, from the sun's decline to sunset
views.case: Later Jewish practice understood the phrase as the afternoon, and the evening offering came to be associated with the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. Luke records 'the hour of prayer, the ninth hour,' Acts 3:1, which fits that practice.

debates.bearing: The precise hour is not the point of the text. The daily offering bracketed Israel's day with worship, and the phrase links it with the Passover slaughter of Exodus 12:6. Whichever reading is right, the evening offering marked the close of every day with atonement and praise.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the pleasing aroma and atonement, several key words shape the chapter.

The 'regular' burnt offering of verses 3, 6, 10, 15 and following is the olat tamid. Tamid means continually or without interruption. It describes the lamps that burn 'continually,' Exodus 27:20, and the altar fire that 'shall be kept burning on the altar continually,' Leviticus 6:13. The word became the name of the daily offering itself; Daniel speaks of an enemy who 'removed His daily sacrifice,' Daniel 8:11, where the Hebrew is simply 'the tamid.' The offerings of this chapter are defined by their constancy.

The animals are to be 'unblemished,' tamim, a similar sounding but different word, meaning complete or whole. It describes Noah as 'blameless in his generation,' Genesis 6:9, and God's call to Abram, 'Walk before Me and be blameless,' Genesis 17:1. The whole animal on the altar pictures the wholeness God seeks in His people, and Malachi 1:8 shows how offering blemished animals despised Him.

In verse 2 God calls the offerings 'My food,' lachmi, from lechem, bread or food. The phrase is not unique; Leviticus 3:11 speaks of fat burned 'as food,' and Leviticus 21:6 of 'the food of their God.' Scripture uses the language while denying that God is hungry, Psalm 50:12 to 13.

'Offering made by fire' translates ishsheh, which appears repeatedly in the chapter. The traditional connection is with esh, fire, and the English follows that. Some scholars connect the word instead with a term for a gift. Either way, it marks what belongs wholly to the LORD.

God's 'appointed time,' verse 2, is moed. The same word appears in Genesis 1:14, where the lights are set 'to mark the seasons,' and it gives the Tent of Meeting its name, the tent of the appointed meeting. The festivals are appointments set by God, and the sanctuary is where He keeps them.

Finally, the male goat 'as a sin offering,' verse 15, is chattat, which is also the ordinary word for sin. The Greek translators often rendered it peri hamartias, 'concerning sin.' Paul uses that phrase when he says God sent His Son 'as an offering for sin,' Romans 8:3, and 2 Corinthians 5:21 goes further: God made Him who knew no sin 'to be sin on our behalf.' The same word that names the offering names what it deals with, and in Christ both come together.

typology.type: The two lambs of the regular offering, morning and twilight
typology.fulfillment: Every day Israel's worship was bracketed by the death of an unblemished lamb, and the fire never went out. John the Baptist points to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and Peter speaks of 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is decisive: the daily lamb covered one day, but Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and then 'sat down,' Hebrews 10:12. The type falls short by its very repetition, for Hebrews says the priests' standing to offer daily shows the work was never finished.

typology.type: The Passover of the fourteenth day, verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The LORD's Passover began the year, recalling the lamb slain 'at twilight' whose blood sheltered Israel in Egypt, Exodus 12:6. Jesus was crucified at Passover, John 19:14, and Paul writes, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The escalation is from escape from Pharaoh to rescue from sin and death. The seven days of unleavened bread that follow are applied to Christian life: 'let us keep the feast... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth,' 1 Corinthians 5:8. The type falls short in that the first Passover delivered one nation for one night; the true one redeems a people from every nation forever.

typology.type: The day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks, verse 26
typology.fulfillment: The offering of new grain was the pledge that the whole harvest belonged to God and would follow. The BSB footnote identifies the feast as Pentecost, and on that day the Spirit was poured out and about three thousand believed, Acts 2:1 and 2:41. Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, believers 'have the firstfruits of the Spirit,' Romans 8:23, and the church is 'a kind of firstfruits of His creation,' James 1:18. The escalation is from a harvest of grain to the resurrection harvest; the type falls short because Israel's firstfruits had to be brought again every year.

typology.type: The goat of the sin offering at each new moon and feast
typology.fulfillment: At each monthly and festival offering a male goat was presented 'to make atonement for you,' verses 22 and 30. The repetition was itself a message; Hebrews says those sacrifices were 'an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,' Hebrews 10:3 to 4. Christ came 'as an offering for sin,' Romans 8:3, and entered the Most Holy Place 'not by the blood of goats and calves' but by His own blood, 'thus securing eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. Where the goat reminded, Christ removes.

typology.type: Sabbath, new moon and appointed feast as a pattern of sacred time
typology.fulfillment: The calendar of Numbers 28 gave all of Israel's time a sacred shape. Paul names the same three terms and says they are 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16 to 17. The rhythms pointed to a rest and a feast that Christ Himself brings, 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9. The shadow is real and God given, but it falls short because it measured time by repetition; in Christ time moves toward its goal, when the city has 'no need... of the sun,' Revelation 22:5.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through its most repeated sight: a lamb on the altar, morning and evening, every day of every year. Israel never lived a day without that death at its centre. The New Testament sees the meaning of that rhythm in Jesus. John introduces Him as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and Isaiah had described the Servant 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7. What the daily offerings did in shadow, covering and consecrating, Christ does in reality.

Hebrews makes the connection most sharply. It pictures the priests at work: 'Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God,' Hebrews 10:11 to 12. The contrast is between standing and sitting, repetition and completion. The olat tamid, the continual offering, could never be finished. Christ's offering is finished and therefore never needs repeating. Hebrews 10:5 to 7 adds that the sacrifices were never what God finally desired; what He desired was a body offered in obedience, and Christ came saying, 'I have come to do Your will, O God.'

The festivals lead to Christ as well, and not by forced allegory, since the New Testament itself draws the lines. Jesus died at Passover, and Paul says, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. He rose as 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The Spirit came at the Feast of Weeks, Acts 2:1, the harvest festival of verse 26, so that the first great ingathering of the church happened on the day Israel offered new grain. The calendar of Numbers 28 turns out to be the calendar of the gospel.

The language of aroma follows the same path. Every offering here is 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD.' Paul says that Christ 'loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. The aroma that rose from the tabernacle every morning and evening pointed to the one life that pleased the Father entirely.

Finally, Christ changes what worship now looks like. Because His sacrifice is complete, His people offer 'a sacrifice of praise' continually, Hebrews 13:15, and their own bodies as 'living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1. The continual offering has not ceased; it has been transformed. At the end, John sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne,' Revelation 5:6. The lamb of the daily offering has become the Lamb on the throne.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who orders time. He set the lights 'to mark the seasons and days and years,' Genesis 1:14, and here He fills those seasons with worship. The day, the week, the month and the year are not neutral units but appointments He sets. The Creator of time claims every part of it.

It shows a God who desires constant fellowship. The daily offering is 'regular,' tamid, without interruption. God does not want to be visited on festival days and forgotten in between. The chapter's refrain, 'in addition to the regular burnt offering,' insists that ordinary days matter to Him as much as feasts. Exodus 29:42 to 45 gives the reason behind it: the daily offering stood 'at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you,' and God promised, 'I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.'

It shows a God who is self sufficient and yet receives gifts. He calls the offerings 'My food,' verse 2, yet Psalm 50:12 reminds Israel that 'the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof.' God does not need Israel's lambs. He invites them to give because giving honours Him and shapes them. The offerings are the grateful return of what He first provided.

It shows a God whose holiness is never suspended. Even the feasts of joy include a goat for atonement. Israel could not presume on His presence, and the atoning offering was part of every celebration. Holiness and joy are not rivals here; holiness makes the joy safe.

It shows a God who provides the way to Himself. Every animal and measure of flour is specified by God, not left to Israel's invention. He prescribes the means by which a sinful people may approach Him, and in doing so He points ahead to the one offering He would provide, as Abraham said long before, 'God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering,' Genesis 22:8.

For worship this chapter teaches regularity, generosity and reverence. It calls believers to meet God daily, not only on special occasions, to bring Him the best rather than the leftover, and to celebrate as people whose sins have been dealt with by the Lamb He provided.

crossReferences.note: The original command for the daily offering, given at Sinai, which Numbers 28:6 says was 'established at Mount Sinai.' Exodus adds that it was offered 'at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you,' so the daily lamb marked the place and time of God's meeting with Israel.

The same feasts described from the people's side: Passover at twilight, Unleavened Bread, the wave sheaf and the count of fifty days to the offering of new grain. Numbers 28 supplies the altar's side, specifying the animals and measures for each day.

God corrects any thought that He needs the offerings Numbers 28:2 calls 'My food': 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine.' The psalm then calls for a sacrifice of thanksgiving, showing the heart God sought behind the calendar.

David prays, 'May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering.' The twilight lamb of Numbers 28:4 and 8 becomes a picture of prayer, showing how Israel already understood the offerings as the expression of a heart turned to God.

God rejects 'your New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations' because they were kept alongside injustice. The calendar of Numbers 28 could be followed to the letter and still be hateful to God, a warning that ritual cannot replace righteousness and mercy.

The returned exiles rebuild the altar before the temple and resume 'the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts.' Restoring Numbers 28 was the first act of a restored people, showing how central the calendar was to Israel's identity.

Daniel foresees a power that 'removed His daily sacrifice and overthrew the place of His sanctuary.' The ending of the tamid, the regular offering of Numbers 28:3, marks the height of desecration. To silence the daily lamb was to strike at the heart of Israel's life with God.

Paul names the same three layers of Israel's calendar, 'a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath,' and calls them 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.' Believers are free from the calendar as law because they possess its substance.

The daily priestly service of Numbers 28 is described exactly: priests stand 'Day after day' to offer 'the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.' Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down, and 'by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.'

Paul calls Christ 'our Passover lamb' and tells the church to 'keep the feast' with 'the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth.' The Passover and seven days of unleavened bread in Numbers 28:16 to 17 become a picture of a whole Christian life lived clean of malice.

The Spirit is poured out 'When the day of Pentecost came,' the Feast of Weeks of Numbers 28:26, as the BSB footnote there notes. The day of firstfruits becomes the day of the first great harvest of the church, when about three thousand believed, Acts 2:41.

Christ 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.' The refrain of Numbers 28, 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD,' finds its fulfilment in the self giving love of the Son, and the church is called to walk in that same love.

'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise.' The continual offering of Numbers 28 is not abolished but transformed: through Christ, God's people offer praise without ceasing, the fruit of lips that confess His name.

study.oneStory:
In the story of creation, fall, redemption and new creation, this chapter shows what redeemed time looks like. At creation God set lights in the sky for 'seasons and days and years,' Genesis 1:14, and rested on the seventh day. Time was made for fellowship with Him. The fall broke that fellowship, and time became a march toward death. Numbers 28 is God's gift of a new rhythm to a redeemed people, a calendar in which every day begins and ends at His altar and every season is marked by His provision and His atonement.

The chapter answers what came before. The first generation had received this pattern at Sinai, verse 6, and then failed in the wilderness and at Peor. The new generation receives it again at the border of the land. God's plan for a worshipping people had not changed, only the people had.

It also sets up what follows in Israel's story. The calendar would be kept in the temple, neglected in times of apostasy, emptied of meaning by hypocrisy, attacked by enemies, and restored by returning exiles. The prophets would expose its misuse and promise a day when all mankind would worship before God from Sabbath to Sabbath. The repetition of the offerings, year after year, kept a question open: when would sin be finally dealt with?

Christ answers that question. He is the Passover lamb, the unblemished offering, the firstfruits of the resurrection, the fragrant sacrifice. His one offering completes what the daily lamb could only repeat. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost begins the great harvest of which Israel's firstfruits were a pledge. Now the church lives by a new rhythm, praising God continually through Jesus and gathering on the first day to remember His death until He comes.

The story ends in the new creation, where the Lord God and the Lamb are the temple of the city, Revelation 21:22. There will be no morning or evening sacrifice, because there will be 'no more night,' Revelation 22:5. The rhythms of Numbers 28 will give way to unbroken fellowship with God, and the continual offering will become continual worship before the Lamb who was slain.

quiz.q: How often was the regular burnt offering of two lambs to be presented, according to verses 3 to 4?

options.text: Every day, one lamb in the morning and one at twilight.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 state this daily rhythm exactly.

options.text: Only once a week, on the Sabbath.
options.note: The Sabbath offering was an addition to, not a replacement for, this daily offering.

options.text: Only once a year, at Passover.
options.note: The daily offering continued every single day, distinct from the annual Passover observance.

options.text: No regular schedule is given.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 give a precise daily schedule.

quiz.q: What was added to the regular burnt offering on the Sabbath, according to verses 9 to 10?

options.text: Two additional unblemished year-old male lambs with their grain and drink offerings.
options.note: Verses 9 to 10 specify this addition on top of the daily offering.

options.text: A complete rest from any offerings at all.
options.note: The Sabbath actually required an additional offering, not a suspension of offerings.

options.text: A single bull offered instead of the usual lambs.
options.note: The text specifies two lambs added for the Sabbath, not a substitution with a bull.

options.text: No addition is specified for the Sabbath.
options.note: Verses 9 to 10 specify the addition in detail.

quiz.q: How many days was the Feast of Unleavened Bread to be observed, according to verse 17?

options.text: Seven days.
options.note: Verse 17 states this length directly.

options.note: The text specifies seven days, not three.

quiz.q: What accompanied the burnt offerings at both the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the Feast of Weeks, according to verses 22 and 30?

quiz.q: What common phrase describes the effect of these burnt offerings throughout the chapter?

options.text: A pleasing aroma to the LORD.
options.note: This phrase recurs repeatedly throughout the chapter, for example verses 2, 6, 8, 13, 24, and 27.

options.text: A burden too heavy for the people to bear.
options.note: The chapter's repeated description is positive, a pleasing aroma, not a burden.

options.text: A sign of coming judgment.
options.note: The offerings are described as pleasing to the LORD, not as signs of judgment.

options.text: No description of their effect is given.
options.note: The phrase pleasing aroma appears repeatedly throughout the chapter.

questions: Israel's worship was structured around daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly rhythms, not left to spontaneous impulse. What regular rhythms of worship shape your own life with God right now?

Even Israel's most joyful festivals included an offering for atonement. Where might you need to bring honest confession into a season of celebration rather than assuming joy and repentance cannot coexist?
The daily lamb offering never lapsed, morning and evening, without fail, for centuries. What would it look like for your own devotion to God to have that same unwavering consistency?
Hebrews contrasts these endlessly repeated sacrifices with Christ's single, sufficient offering. Where are you still trying to repeatedly earn what Christ has already accomplished once for all?

This whole calendar of offerings was preparing Israel to worship faithfully once they were settled and comfortable in the land. What practices keep your own worship from growing careless once life becomes comfortable?

translationNotes.note: An ephah and a hin are ancient dry and liquid measures respectively; a tenth of an ephah of flour and a quarter hin of oil represent modest, carefully fixed quantities rather than open-ended amounts, ensuring consistency across every offering.

Fermented drink translates a Hebrew term for strong drink poured out as a drink offering; unlike offerings eaten or burned, this liquid offering was entirely poured out, symbolizing a gift wholly given with nothing kept back.

The LORD's Passover and the following Feast of Unleavened Bread, though distinct in origin, Exodus 12, are treated here as a combined eight-day observance, reflecting how closely the two had become joined in Israel's actual practice by this point.
